Coypu (Myocastor coypus) is a large semi-aquatic rodent native to South America that has established invasive populations across temperate regions worldwide. Parturition typically produces a litter of six pups [N_R_i = Parturition typically produces a litter of six pups], a value that represents the maximum reproductive output recorded for this species in its native range. Females can produce multiple litters annually, with the maximum observed rate corresponding to approximately 2.3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.3 litters per year], a reproductive frequency that provides remarkable colonizing potential. These reproductive parameters have been documented at a core body temperature of 34.6 °C [T = 34.6 °C], reflecting the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species. The combination of moderate litter size and frequent breeding events underpins the coypu's well-documented capacity for rapid population growth in newly colonized habitats, a trait that has frustrated control efforts from the Gulf Coast of the United States to the wetlands of northern Europe.

At birth, coypu neonates exhibit a wet body mass of approximately 225 grams [Wwb = approximately 225 grams], a value that positions them among the larger newborn rodents relative to adult size. These precocial young are fully furred, have their eyes open at parturition, and are capable of swimming within hours of birth, representing a substantial maternal investment. The gestation period that precedes this live birth event lasts approximately 131 days [tg = approximately 131 days] under the same thermal regime of 34.6 °C [T = 34.6 °C], an exceptionally long pregnancy for a rodent of this size. In comparative context, the gestation length of the coypu exceeds that of the similarly sized muskrat by a considerable margin, reflecting the advanced developmental state of the neonates at delivery. This extended pregnancy is metabolically demanding for the gravid female, who must sustain both her own maintenance requirements and the rapid foetal development characteristic of this species' reproductive strategy.

Lactation in the coypu supports a suckling juvenile through a developmental period that culminates in weaning relatively early compared to the extended gestation. The weaning process, marking the transition from complete maternal milk dependence to nutritional independence, occurs at approximately 91 days after birth [tx = approximately 91 days after birth] under the thermal conditions of 34.6 °C [T = 34.6 °C], at which point the offspring have reached a wet body weight of around 1750 grams [Wwx = around 1750 grams]. This body mass at the cessation of nursing represents roughly a 7.8-fold increase over the birth weight, highlighting the rapid somatic growth achieved during the suckling phase. The post-weaning juvenile then enters a period of continued growth and development, gradually transitioning from the protective maternal environment to the more demanding conditions experienced by independent young in the aquatic marshland habitats this species typically occupies.

The timing of sexual maturation in coypu is notably delayed relative to many other rodent species of comparable body size. Puberty is attained approximately 152 days after birth [tp = approximately 152 days after birth] when maintained at the typical active body temperature of 34.6 °C [T = 34.6 °C], a duration that reflects the substantial somatic growth required before reproductive activation can commence. By this stage of sexual maturation, individuals have achieved most of their structural growth, although they continue to add mass after reaching reproductive maturity. The maximum adult wet body weight attained by females under favorable conditions approaches 7850 grams [Wwi = 7850 grams], positioning the species as one of the largest rodents in its ecological guild. Reaching this ultimate body mass requires sustained access to high-quality forage, and individuals in marginal habitats often plateau at lower asymptotic weights.

Longevity data for coypu from both wild and captive settings indicate that the average maximum lifespan rarely exceeds approximately eight and a half years (8.5 years) [am = 8.5 years] when maintained at a core body temperature around 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a thermoregulatory set point typical of inactive or resting periods. This lifespan estimate, derived from captive colony records, places the species among the longer-lived members of the family Echimyidae, and within the range observed for other large caviomorph rodents such as capybaras and porcupines, though it is considerably shorter than the maximum longevity documented in the related hystricognath genus Hydrochoerus. The ecological mortality experienced by free-ranging individuals is of course substantially higher, with few wild coypus surviving beyond their third year due to predation pressure, harsh winter conditions, and disease outbreaks that can decimate local populations in the temperate wetlands they inhabit across their wide geographic distribution.
